statement of the hypothesis under test

spans.assertion: the analysis examined whether red card issuance differs by player skin tone using 110,151 player-referee dyads across four European leagues (England, France, Germany, Spain) for the 2012-2013 season
adjusted for exposure (number of games), player position, league, height, and weight using logistic regression with clustered standard errors
found an adjusted risk difference of 0.1875 percentage points (95% CI -0.0069 to 0.4047; p=0.0705)
found an adjusted odds ratio of 1.161 (95% CI 0.997-1.353; p=0.0550)
concluded overall that the hypothesis is NOT SUPPORTED
point estimates suggest a small positive association between dark skin tone and red card probability that is not statistically significant at α=0.05
evidence is insufficient to conclude referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players

spans.note: section divider and DETAILED RESULTS header

spans.assertion: reports detailed risk-difference statistics: point estimate 0.1875pp, SE 0.1036pp, 95% CI [-0.0069,0.4047], p=0.0705, alpha=0.05

dark-skinned players have an estimated 0.19 percentage-point higher probability of a red card than light-skinned players after adjusting for covariates, but the difference is not statistically significant (p=0.071)
marginal standardization predicts red-card risk of 1.391% if all players were dark-skinned vs 1.204% if all were light-skinned, a difference of 0.188pp
the risk-difference CI [-0.007,0.405] includes zero, so the null hypothesis of no difference cannot be rejected at α=0.05
reports detailed odds-ratio statistics: point estimate 1.161, 95% CI [0.997,1.353], p=0.0550
odds of a red card are 16.1% higher for dark-skinned than light-skinned players, not statistically significant at α=0.05 (p=0.055)
the odds-ratio CI [0.997,1.353] barely includes 1.0, indicating marginal evidence of an effect
defined the unit of analysis as player-referee dyads, each aggregating all games between one player and one referee
the dataset comprises 110,151 dyads, 1,345 unique players, 2,862 unique referees, representing 357,131 total games
sample composition: 83,655 light-skin dyads (75.9%) with 1,016 red cards (1.215%); 26,496 dark-skin dyads (24.1%) with 358 red cards (1.351%); unadjusted risk difference 0.137pp
defined the outcome as a binary indicator of whether the player received any red card across all encounters with the referee
red cards are rare, occurring in only 1.25% of dyads
two independent raters, blind to the research question, coded player skin tone from profile photos
skin tone was coded on what is described as a 5-point scale ranging from 0 (very light) to 1 (very dark)
computed the final skin tone measure by averaging the two raters' scores
dichotomized skin tone into light (≤0.25) and dark (≥0.5) categories
excluded players with middle skin tones (0.25<tone<0.5) to obtain a clearer contrast between groups
adjusted for the natural log of number of games in the dyad as the key exposure variable
adjusted for player position using 12 categories
adjusted for league country (England, France, Germany, Spain)
adjusted for standardized player height
adjusted for standardized player weight
fit a logistic regression of P(any red card) on the dark-skin indicator plus covariates
estimated the model via maximum likelihood
clustered standard errors at the player level to account for within-player correlation across dyads
used statsmodels 0.14 in Python for estimation
the model converged successfully in 9 iterations
model fit statistics: pseudo R²=0.095, log-likelihood=-6684.2

spans.note: lead-in noting full model coefficients are in supplementary output

spans.assertion: dark_skin coefficient β=0.1497, SE=0.078, p=0.055
log_games coefficient β=0.980, SE=0.029, p<0.001, described as a strong exposure effect
used marginal standardization (g-computation) to estimate the risk difference by predicting red-card probability under dark_skin=1 and dark_skin=0 and differencing the means
computed the confidence interval via parametric bootstrap: 2,000 coefficient vectors sampled from the estimated MVN distribution, RD computed for each, CI taken from the 2.5th/97.5th percentiles
the original dataset contained 146,028 dyads
excluded 21,407 dyads (14.7%) with missing skin-tone ratings due to no photo
excluded 5,609 dyads (4.0%) with middle skin tones
excluded 8,108 dyads (6.1%) with missing position data
excluded 799 dyads (0.6%) with missing height/weight data
the final analysis sample comprised 110,151 dyads, 75.4% of the original dataset
standardized height and weight to mean 0, SD 1
log-transformed the number of games to address right skew
the games variable had a median of 1 and a maximum of 47

spans.note: section divider and SENSITIVITY ANALYSES header

spans.assertion: states that the primary analysis was robust to alternative specifications
modeled skin tone as a continuous variable (0-1) instead of dichotomous, as a sensitivity check
the continuous skin-tone model gave coefficient 0.224, p=0.052
odds ratio per 0.1 increase in continuous skin tone was 1.023
the continuous-model result showed a similar pattern to the main analysis, marginally non-significant
used an alternative dichotomization (median split: dark >0.25 vs light ≤0.25) for more balanced groups as a sensitivity check
alternative dichotomization gave coefficient 0.150, p=0.055, OR=1.161
result of alternative dichotomization was identical to the main analysis, confirming robustness
examined the effect stratified by exposure (number of games played) as a sensitivity check
risk difference by games-played stratum: 0.137pp (N=110,151, ≥1 game), 0.228pp (N=54,559, ≥2), 0.272pp (N=36,622, ≥3), 0.238pp (N=20,899, ≥5)
effect was slightly larger with more exposure but remained small
the effect was heterogeneous across leagues
risk difference by league: England +0.316pp (N=30,625), Germany +0.399pp (N=37,174), France -0.537pp (N=16,303), Spain -0.255pp (N=26,049)
direction of the effect varies by country, suggesting context-dependent effects
unadjusted odds ratio was 1.114
adjusted odds ratio was 1.161
adjustment changed the odds ratio by +4.3%
comparison of unadjusted vs adjusted estimates indicates minimal confounding, with adjustment slightly increasing the estimate

spans.note: section divider and LIMITATIONS AND POTENTIAL BIASES header

spans.assertion: the analysis aggregates data at the dyad level across multiple games between a player and referee
using a binary outcome (any red card) loses information about frequency
cannot assess game-specific factors such as match importance, score, crowd, or timing
temporal dynamics within games were not captured
did not adjust for playing style, aggression, or disciplinary history
player position serves only as a crude proxy for playing style
had no data on individual referee characteristics or implicit bias
had no data on player reputation or previous player-referee encounters
cannot establish a causal relationship from this observational data
residual confounding likely biases estimates in an unknown direction
data is from the 2012-2013 season only and may not reflect current patterns
analysis is limited to four European leagues (England, France, Germany, Spain)
results may not generalize to other leagues, time periods, or sports
excluding middle skin tones limits inference to the extremes of the skin-tone distribution
red card outcome is rare, about 1.2% overall
the analysis may be underpowered to detect small effects
wide confidence intervals reflect substantial uncertainty
effect size is small (0.19pp), requiring large samples to detect
adjusted standard errors for player-level clustering
did not adjust for referee-level clustering
some referees may have systematically different thresholds for giving red cards
did not model the cross-classified structure of players nested in referees and vice versa
standard errors may be slightly underestimated
conducted five sensitivity analyses
did not adjust p-values for multiple testing
risk of false positives increases with the number of tests conducted

spans.note: generic caution recommending caution interpreting borderline p-values

spans.assertion: country-level bias measures (meanIAT, meanExp) were available but not used
individual referee bias was not measured

spans.note: generic caveat that aggregate measures may not reflect individual behavior

spans.assertion: the cross-sectional observational design precludes causal inference
cannot rule out reverse causation or bidirectional effects
experimental manipulation was not used because it was not feasible

spans.note: section divider and KEY ASSUMPTIONS header

spans.assertion: assumed missing-at-random: players with missing photos do not differ systematically from those with photos in red-card rates, conditional on covariates
assessed the MAR assumption as uncertain, since it cannot be tested without data on missing players
if the MAR assumption is violated, selection bias could distort estimates in an unknown direction
assumed no unmeasured confounding: conditional on covariates, skin tone is independent of red-card propensity
assessed the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption as likely violated because playing style and aggression were not measured
residual confounding may bias estimates in either direction, so causal interpretation is not warranted
assumed logistic regression with linear covariate effects is appropriate and that no important interactions or non-linearities were omitted
assessed the model-specification assumption as reasonable, supported by sensitivity checks with continuous skin tone and an appropriate log transformation of games
robustness checks suggest any misspecification bias has minimal impact
assumed dyads are independent after conditioning on player via clustering
assessed the independence assumption as partially met: player-level clustering adjusted but not referee-level, so dyads sharing a referee may be correlated
standard errors may be slightly underestimated and confidence intervals may be too narrow as a result
assumed skin tone was measured with equal accuracy for all players (non-differential measurement error)
assessed the measurement-error assumption as uncertain: raters were blind to outcome, but photo quality may vary
non-differential error would bias estimates toward the null (conservative); differential error could bias in either direction
assumed the sample size was sufficient for the asymptotic properties of MLE and bootstrap to hold
assessed the large-sample assumption as met, since N=110,151 is large and convergence was successful
minimal concern for the validity of inference results from this
final answer to the primary research question is 'not supported'
restates an adjusted risk difference of 0.19pp (95% CI -0.01 to 0.40, p=0.071), suggesting dark-skinned players have marginally higher red-card rates
this finding is not statistically significant at α=0.05; the CI includes zero and the p-value (0.071) exceeds the significance threshold
adjusted odds ratio of 1.16 (95% CI 1.00-1.35, p=0.055) also fails to reach statistical significance, with both estimates described as borderline
substantive effect is small: red-card rate rises from 1.20% (light-skinned) to 1.39% (dark-skinned), a 0.19pp difference representing a 16% relative increase in odds but minimal absolute change

sensitivity analyses reveal heterogeneity by league (positive associations in England/Germany, negative in France/Spain), suggesting context-dependent effects possibly reflecting refereeing culture, league composition, or unmeasured factors

overall evidence is deemed insufficient to conclude referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players, citing lack of significance, small effect with wide CIs, potential confounding, missing data (~15%), and heterogeneity
cannot rule out a small effect, but the data do not convincingly support the hypothesis at the conventional significance level; p-values (0.055-0.071) are described as suggestive but not conclusive
a conservative interpretation is warranted: the hypothesis is not supported
additional research with game-level data, playing-style/aggression measures, referee characteristics, larger or experimental samples, and more recent data would strengthen inference
even if the effect were real, its absolute magnitude is very small: for a player with 30 games, red-card probability rises from 0.36% to 0.42% (0.06pp), roughly 1 additional red card per 1,600 games
